summary: Psalm 42 opens Book II of Psalms with a speaker longing for God as intensely as a thirsty deer longs for water. The speaker remembers leading a joyful crowd to God’s house, but now lives with tears, distance, enemies, and the repeated taunt, “Where is your God?” Twice the psalm turns inward with the same refrain, calling the distressed self to hope in God and expect future praise.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Psalms gives words for longing, memory, protest, and hope in the same prayer. It also begins the Korahite material in Book II and introduces a refrain that continues into Psalm 43.

context.author: The heading says, “A contemplation by the sons of Korah.” In Psalms, headings are ancient parts of the transmitted collection, but their exact historical force can be debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the psalms for public and private prayer.
context.date: Individual psalms come from different periods, and the five-book Psalter is a later anthology; one precise date for Psalm 42 is not established by the chapter.
context.setting: The speaker remembers God’s house and a festive crowd, while now speaking from distress and from places named as the land of the Jordan, Hermon, and Mizar.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, using vivid images, repeated questions, direct address to God, and a refrain addressed to the speaker’s own soul.

outline.heading: Thirst for God
outline.note: The psalm opens with a heading, then compares the speaker’s desire for God to a deer panting for water.

outline.heading: Tears and Memory
outline.note: The speaker’s grief is sharpened by taunts and by remembering former worship with the crowd at God’s house.

outline.heading: First Refrain of Hope
outline.note: The speaker questions the despair within and calls the soul to hope in God.

outline.heading: Overwhelmed but Praying
outline.note: The speaker remembers God from distant places, feels swept over by waves, and still speaks of Yahweh’s loving kindness and song.

outline.heading: Complaint Under Reproach
outline.note: The speaker asks why God seems to have forgotten him while enemies continue their painful taunt.

outline.heading: Second Refrain of Hope
outline.note: The chapter closes by repeating the inward question and the call to hope in God.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. A contemplation by the sons of Korah. As the deer pants for the water brooks, so my soul pants after you, God.
keyVerses.why: This verse supplies the heading and the central opening image: deep thirst for God.

keyVerses.text: My tears have been my food day and night, while they continually ask me, “Where is your God?”
keyVerses.why: It names both the speaker’s grief and the repeated challenge from others.

keyVerses.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him for the saving help of his presence.
keyVerses.why: This refrain gives the psalm its internal dialogue: despair is real, but the speaker commands the self to hope.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh will command his loving kindness in the daytime. In the night his song shall be with me: a prayer to the God of my life.
keyVerses.why: In the middle of distress, the speaker still speaks of Yahweh’s loving kindness, song, and prayer.

questions.question: Who are the “sons of Korah”?
questions.answer: The chapter’s heading associates this psalm with the sons of Korah, but the chapter itself does not explain who they are. In the Psalter, headings may indicate collection, performance, dedication, authorship, or association, so readers should treat the heading as important evidence without pressing it into one certain modern category.

questions.question: What does “contemplation” mean here?
questions.answer: The heading calls the psalm “A contemplation,” but the chapter does not define the term. It signals a type or use of psalm, while the poem itself shows a reflective prayer moving through longing, memory, complaint, and hope.

questions.question: Why does the psalm compare the speaker to a deer?
questions.answer: The comparison is about intense need. As a deer pants for water brooks, the speaker’s soul pants for God, and the next verse says, “My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.”

questions.question: Is the speaker angry at God, or still trusting God?
questions.answer: The chapter includes both complaint and trust. The speaker asks, “Why have you forgotten me?” and also calls God “my rock,” speaks of Yahweh’s loving kindness, and tells the soul to hope in God. The psalm does not treat honest questioning and hope as opposites.

questions.question: What has the speaker lost or been separated from?
questions.answer: The speaker remembers going with the crowd to God’s house with joy, praise, and a holy day. The chapter does not give the exact reason for the present separation, but it makes clear that former public worship is now painful to remember.

questions.question: Why do others ask, “Where is your God?”
questions.answer: The question appears as a taunt in verses 3 and 10. The speaker’s tears, mourning, and oppression make enemies or adversaries use the situation to challenge God’s presence or help. The psalm reports the wound of the question without explaining who these adversaries are.

questions.question: Why does the speaker talk to his own soul?
questions.answer: The speaker turns inward and questions the despair within: “Why are you in despair, my soul?” This is a poetic way of naming inner turmoil and answering it with a call to hope in God. The repetition in verses 5 and 11 makes this self-address one of the chapter’s main features.

questions.question: What do the waves and waterfalls mean?
questions.answer: Verse 7 uses water imagery very differently from the opening thirst image. Instead of desired water, the speaker describes being overwhelmed: “All your waves and your billows have swept over me.” The chapter presents distress as something powerful and engulfing.

questions.question: Does the psalm end with the problem solved?
questions.answer: No outward rescue is narrated in this chapter. The enemies are still present in verse 10, and the final verse repeats the question about despair. What changes is not the situation but the speaker’s repeated refusal to let despair have the last word.

glossary.def: The speaker’s inner life or whole needy self, addressed directly in the poem as thirsty, despairing, disturbed, and called to hope.
The way verse 2 names the God for whom the speaker thirsts, emphasizing God as the one sought in worship and prayer.
The place the speaker remembers going with a joyful crowd, praise, and a holy day.
Large waves; in verse 7 they are part of the image of being overwhelmed by distress.
The daytime gift the speaker says Yahweh will command, paired with song in the night and prayer to the God of his life.
